 Taro is believed
to have been brought to Hawaii between
400 and 500 A.D. by the first Marquesan
and Tahitian settlers.  According to
Hawaiian tradition, taro is the staff of
life.  Taro also was carried westward to
Arabia and was an important crop in the
Nile Valley by 500 B.C.  Today, taro is a
staple in the diets of the people of West
Africa, the Caribbean, and the Polynesian
Islands.  It is grown throughout tropical
and subtropical Asia and the Pacific and
in parts of Africa and the Americas.
Taro is a succulent perennial plant
that ranges in height from about 20 inch-
es to 6 feet.  Young corms develop as off-
shoots of the main corm and can produce
new plants.  Although taro is generally
regarded as a bog plant, it can grow in a
variety of environments from dry ground
to wetlands and can tolerate lighting
conditions ranging from deep shade to
bright sunlight. Because taro seeds and
seedlings do not survive well and the
plants rarely flower, propagation is done
primarily by planting side corms or by
cutting off and planting the top of a large
tuber with its shoot.
Uses

to neutralize the toxic calcium oxalate
